preserved_objections.basis: The proposed mechanism increases thermal loading which accelerates potential-induced degradation, directly contradicting the goal of extending module lifespan in high-voltage string configurations.

The candidate specifies deployment in high-temperature environments with optimal reflector angle of 30°, but fails to account for seasonal variations in sun angle that would make this angle suboptimal for much of the year, violating the boundary condition of consistent performance.

The candidate's own evidence [doi:10.1038/s41598-026-49258-9] shows reflector materials increase module temperature by 8-12°C, which directly contradicts the claim that the design mitigates thermal stress while simultaneously predicting accelerated degradation from increased thermal loading.

The candidate fails to demonstrate any improvement over baseline modules, as the increased energy capture from reflected light is negated by the accelerated degradation from thermal stress and sodium ion migration, resulting in net zero benefit.

The proposed reflector materials (aluminum foil, galvanized steel, and mirror) have vastly different degradation rates and maintenance requirements in outdoor environments, making consistent implementation impossible without regular replacement that would negate any economic benefit.

The testable prediction of measuring sodium ion migration rates requires destructive testing of modules, making it impossible to measure in deployed systems while the module is still generating power, rendering the prediction practically untestable in real-world conditions.
